May 19, 2026 4 CONSENT AGENDA INFORMATION In an effort to streamline Annual Town Meeting and make it more accessible and efficient for voters, the Select Board will again use Consent Agendas. This process helps expedite the passage of articles that the Select Board, after consulting with Town Counsel, the Moderator, and the Finance Committee, believes are not expected to generate controversy and may appropriately be acted upon without debate. The purpose of a Consent Agenda is to allow motions under designated articles to be considered together as one unit and voted on without debate. This year, there will be 5 Consent Agendas: 1. Non-Financial Consent Agenda (Articles 13 through 14)1 Includes routine administrative and procedural articles that do not involve financial appropriations and are not expected to require discussion. 2. Financial (Non-Capital) Consent Agenda (Articles 15 through 24) 2 Includes non-capital financial articles such as standard financial and administrative items, operational and maintenance expenses, employee-related costs, public safety needs, and other standard financial and compliance items. 3. Capital Consent Agenda (Articles 26 through 41) 3 Includes capital purchases and projects such as equipment, technology, facility improvements, and public safety investments that support ongoing Town operations and infrastructure. 4. Two-Thirds Vote Articles (Articles 42 through 43) 4 Includes articles that require a two-thirds vote under Massachusetts General Law. While grouped for efficiency, each article within this Consent Agenda will still require a two-thirds vote for passage. 5. Community Preservation Committee (CPC) Consent Agenda (Articles 44 through 50) 5 Includes Community Preservation Act projects related to open space, historic preservation, community housing, and recreation, as recommended through the Community Preservation Committee process. At the call of each Consent Agenda, the Moderator will announce the number of each article. If one or more voters object to including any particular article in the Consent Agenda, they should say the word “Hold” in a loud voice when the number is called. That article will then be removed from the Consent Agenda and restored to its original place in the Warrant, where it will be debated and voted on in the usual manner. After all articles in the Consent Agenda have been called, the Moderator will ask that all remaining articles be voted as a unit. Voters are encouraged to carefully review the list of articles proposed for each Consent Agenda. Summaries are included under each article as printed in this Warrant. 2026 Annual Town Meeting (FY27) Warrant - May 19, 2026 5 May 19, 2026 Tellers were sworn in: Kim Grotbek, Cassie LaRussa, John Fallon, Tim Rudolph, Leah Wofsy and Justin Rowe. Election workers were sworn in: Karen Whitcomb, Anne McNeece, Carol Driscoll, and Elizabeth Nichols. Annual Town Meeting was called to order by Elected Town Meeting Moderator, Dennis Reip at 7:06 pm. A total of 161 registered voters checked in (3.9% of 4,087 registered voters). There was only one night of Town Meeting this year. Opening Ceremony: All stood for our National Anthem performed by the Blanchard Memorial Vocal Ensemble under the direction of Margie Callaghan and accompanied by 6th Grader Zoe Li. Daria Kochurova lead us in the voluntary Pledge of Allegiance. Moderator Reip thanked the students for leading us. Introductions: Mr. Reip introduced Town Clerk Rebecca Harris, Town Counsel Joe Fair, and Town Administrator Michael Johns. He introduced the Boxborough Select Board Chair, Kristin Hilberg, and the members introduced themselves: Clerk, Bob Stemple, Priya Sundaram, Wes Fowlks, and Sam Anderson. He introduced the Finance Committee Chair, Antony Newton, and the members introduced themselves: John Connor, Vice Chair and Clerk, John Greven, Maria Neyland, and Joseph Stulpin. Michelle Ryan was absent. Administrative Assistant, Kelley Price, and Town Planner, Alec Wade were introduced, running the projector, showing the motions and presentations on the screen. He introduced the town Finance Director Honghoa Le to assist with any financial facts of the matter. He recognized that Rajon Hudson, Assistant Town Administrator is not present due to being with his family as his mother receives end of life care. In the front row of chairs are members of the School Committee and Planning Board There are numerous town department heads and staff, our chiefs of police and fire, as well as members of volunteer boards and committees on hand to speak to some of the motions as needed. This meeting is being broadcast live and is also being recorded for on demand viewing on BXB-TV by Littleton Community Television (LCTV). Mr. Reip expressed his thanks to LCTV's Executive Director Mark Crory, LCTV’s Video Program Coordinator Judy Reid and Nick Casteletto and the rest of their crew. On behalf of the Town, Mr. Reip extended thanks to the Blanchard School’s principal Michael Votto for being a gracious host and Blanchard School’s Dan Ralls and his staff and to Ed Kukkula and our DPW staff for preparing the gym for tonight’s Town Meeting. 2026 Annual Town Meeting (FY27) Warrant - May 19, 2026 6 Announcements Non-voters over the age of 18 need to sit in the BACK of the hall in the area marked off to the side on the right as you are facing the stage. Refreshments at the back of the hall are being provided by the Boxborough Conservation Trust. Town Meeting will be tonight, and if voters approve the proposed procedural motion a bit later on, will continue, if needed, to tomorrow Wednesday May 20th and Thursday May 21st if needed. Boxborough’s Municipal Election is TUESDAY, June 2nd, 7:00 am to 8:00 pm at Town Hall. There are contested races for seats on the Select Board, Planning Board, and School Committee along with unopposed candidates seeking re-election to the Board of Health, Library Trustees, and Town Moderator positions. Please consider the candidates and VOTE next week. He went on to explain Town Meeting process. The agenda for this meeting is the Warrant. Everything we discuss at this meeting is contained in the warrant. This is not a public hearing or forum for random matters of interest and we will not be discussing anything that is not already identified in the Warrant. The Warrant includes summaries and recommendations for each article. In addition to the Warrant, material on the tables in the back of room includes a postcard with a QR code to the detailed FY26 school budget book, the 2025 Town Report, a Resident Survey QR code, and a Guide to Town Meeting. Mr. Reip explained that his job as Moderator is to be the presiding officer of this legislature. The Boxborough Town Meeting process is guided by Town Meeting Time, a handbook of parliamentary law prepared by the Massachusetts Moderators Association. He is here to ensure that Town Meeting is: Fair: There is a set of rules and everyone follows them Open: Everyone who wishes to speak has the opportunity to do so Civil: Everyone listens respectfully. One part of being civil is that there is no applause or booing during discussion of articles. Relevant: All the discussion, motions, and amendments must be “within the four corners” of the motion on the floor, and voters must be notified in advance of the items to be discussed at Town Meeting by way of the Warrant. We vote on MOTIONS which might be slightly different from the wording of the Articles printed in the warrant. The motions will be displayed on the screen. Starting on page 8 of the Warrant you will find the Town Meeting Guide which summarizes the process with some of the most common motions listed. Voters were given a 1-page handout on “Boxborough Town Meeting Process” as they walked in. Four key points: a) To be recognized to speak you need to be at one of the two microphones. 2026 Annual Town Meeting (FY27) Warrant - May 19, 2026 7 b) Speakers must state their name and address for the record and are limited to 3 minutes. There will be a clock for all to see here up on the screen. c) All discussion must be relevant to the Motions on the floor d) Mr. Reip will call for a vote when no one is standing at microphone. If someone wants to end debate before that they need to come to a microphone and say “I move the question” and we will vote on stopping debate. Sponsors of the article cannot move the question. Voters cannot make comments at the mic, and then immediately move the question. Mr. Reip may call for votes to be made simply by voice, yea or nay, or a show of hands using the green cards, or if necessary, by a standing count. All voters should have received a “bright green” card when you signed in. For anything other than a voice vote, you need to have a green card to vote and for your vote to be counted. When he asks for a vote by a show of hands, he will ask you to raise the card to make it easier for to see. If we go to a standing count, he’ll ask you to show your card to be counted. Under town bylaw Mr. Reip has the ability to declare a majority or a 2/3 vote using the voice vote or show of hands vote methods. If he does so, and seven voters think he was in error, please say so immediately and we will have a standing counted vote instead. Note: if anyone has a question about process you can stand in place at any time and say “Point of Order” in a loud voice and direct your question to the Moderator. Except for a point of order, you MUST be at a microphone to ask a question, make a comment, or make a motion to move the question. We will have two microphones tonight and I will be recognizing people to speak in an alternating fashion. I will refer to these as the microphone to my right (your left), and the microphone to my left (your right). Please note the chairs along the aisles directly behind each microphone that are intended for people waiting in line at the microphones. Please leave these seats open for folks lining up to speak. Please remember to keep the discussion CIVIL and disagree without being disagreeable. Boxborough has a long tradition of civility at TM. Let’s continue this tradition here tonight. Consent Agendas: In an effort to streamline Town Meeting, we will continue with the use of Consent Agendas. The Consent Agendas are intended to speed the passage of articles that have already been discussed at previous public meetings, and have the unanimous recommendation of both the Select Board and Finance Committee. This consent process allows for motions under these articles to be acted upon as one unit and to be passed without debate. He stated that he would be taking a different approach from past reports, highlighting this pivotal moment, rather than the past year’s accomplishments. Our enrollment has dropped by 600 students and because we are a wealthy town we don’t get a lot of state aid. He spoke about how the budget is put together. There have been double-digit increases in health insurance, retirement, state-mandated tuition, and other costs. Cuts were made in 2022 through 2024. They reduced spending and classroom assistants, and finally teaching positions and basic supplies. The previous year’s Elementary Budget Task Force reduced classroom assistants and shared specialized staff across schools. The class sizes are pushing the limits of the school committee guidelines. The committee engaged the community throughout the process. More than 6,000 survey responses have been received, over 1,000 emails received, and over 20 hours of public comments and questions. text: Annual Town Meeting, May 12, 2026 TOWN OF BOXFORD Website: BoxfordMA.gov Warrant for Annual Town Meeting Tuesday, May 12, 2026 7:00 p.m. Masconomet Regional High School 20 Endicott Road Boxford, MA 01921 Supporting documents for this warrant may be found at: https://www.boxfordma.gov/TownMeeting2026 WARRANT FOR ANNUAL TOWN MEETING May 12, 2026 - 7:00 P.M. 1 Annual Town Meeting, May 12, 2026 MASCONOMET REGIONAL HIGH SCHOOL – AUDITORIUM Commonwealth of Massachusetts Essex s.s. To either of the Constables of the Town of Boxford in said County, GREETINGS: In the name of the Commonwealth of Massachusetts, you are hereby directed to notify and warn the inhabitants of the Town of Boxford qualified to vote in elections and in Town affairs to meet at the Masconomet Regional High School, 20 Endicott Road, Boxford, on Tuesday the twelfth day of May next at 7:00 P.M., then and there to act on the following articles, viz: ARTICLE 1. To receive and place on file the reports of the Town Officers and Committees without ratification of any action taken or authorization of any action proposed; or take any other action thereon. Sponsored and Supported by the Select Board ARTICLE 2. To see if the Town, in accordance with M.G.L. Chapter 150E, section 7, will vote to appropriate a sum of money to fund the first-year cost items contained in the following collective bargaining agreements recently negotiated and ratified by the Select Board between the Town and the following Unions which have terms of July 1, 2026 through June 30, 2029: • • • • American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees, AFL-CIO Council #93, Local 939, Clerical/ Library International Association of Fire Fighters, AFL-CIO Local 5305, Boxford Professional Fire Fighters Boxford Police Officers’ Association, Massachusetts Coalition of Police Boxford Police Reserve Association Said collective bargaining agreements are on file with the Town Clerk; funding for the cost items in the first year of said agreements is included in the general operating budgets of the Town; or take any other action thereon. Sponsored by the Select Board Select Board to make recommendation at Town Meeting Finance Committee to make recommendation at Town Meeting ARTICLE 3. To see if the Town will vote to adopt the Classification Plan and Compensation Plan for FY 2027, as submitted under Chapter 23 of the Town Code; said Classification Plan and Compensation Plan as printed on pages 13 through 15 of this warrant; funding for estimated costs of said plan is included in the general operating budget of Town in Article 4; or take any other action thereon. Sponsored and Supported by the Select Board Finance Committee recommends adoption of this article 2 Annual Town Meeting, May 12, 2026 ARTICLE 4. To act on the proposed budget and see what sums of money the Town will vote to raise and appropriate, or transfer from available funds, for the use of several departments for Fiscal Year 2027, to wit: General Government, Land Use, Building and Health, Human Services, Culture and Recreation, Public Works and Facilities, Public Safety, and Education, and all other necessary proper expenses during said fiscal year; and authorize expenditure of these funds under the direction of the appropriate listed department; or take any other action thereon. Sponsored and Supported by the Finance Committee Estimate: $47,120,570 Select Board recommends adoption of this article The proposed budget is printed on pages 11 and 12 of this warrant. ARTICLE 5. To see if the Town will vote to transfer and appropriate from Free Cash the sum of $128,943 (Boxford’s 37% share of total) to be expended by the Masconomet Regional School District Committee, at the advice of the School Superintendent, to complete various capital projects, including replacing Chromebooks, renovating the Middle School Sidewalk or take any other action thereon. Sponsored and supported by the Masconomet Regional District School Committee Finance Committee recommends adoption of this article Select Board recommends adoption of this article ARTICLE 6. To see if the Town will approve the $1,738,652 borrowing, consisting of $698,938 for Masconomet High School and $1,039,714 for Masconomet Middle School, authorized by the Masconomet Regional School District (the “District”), for the purpose of paying feasibility study and schematic design costs related to a potential Accelerated Repair Project involving replacement of the roof and conversion of the HVAC system to heat pumps at Masconomet Middle School, located at 20 Endicott Rd in Boxford, MA, and replacement of the roof and conversion of the HVAC system to heat pumps at Masconomet High School, located at 20 Endicott Rd. in Boxford, MA, including the payment of all costs incidental or related thereto (the “Project”), which proposed repair project would materially extend the useful life of the school and preserve an asset that otherwise is capable of supporting the required educational program, and for which the District may be eligible for a school construction grant from the Massachusetts School Building Authority (the “MSBA”), said amount to be expended at the direction of the Masconomet Regional District School Committee. The MSBA’s grant program is a non-entitlement, discretionary program based on need, as determined by the MSBA, and any Project costs the District incurs in excess of any grant approved by and received from the MSBA shall be the sole responsibility of the District and its member municipalities. Sponsored and supported by the Masconomet Regional School District School Committee Finance Committee recommends adoption of this article Select Board recommends adoption of this article ARTICLE 7. To act on the list of proposed equipment and capital purchases and see what sums of money the Town will vote to transfer from available Free Cash, for the use of several departments, and authorize expenditure of these funds for such purposes under the direction of the appropriate listed department and authorize the Select Board or School Committee to dispose of any equipment declared surplus if replaced; or take any other action thereon. Sponsored and supported by the Select Board 3 Annual Town Meeting, May 12, 2026 Estimate: $355,901 Finance Committee recommends adoption of this article The proposed capital budget is printed on page 16 of this warrant. Permanent Building Committee recommendations as noted on page 16. School Committee recommendations as noted on page 16. ARTICLE 8. To see if the town will vote to transfer and appropriate from Free Cash the sum of $345,000 to the Finance Committee Reserve line item in the current Fiscal Year 2026 budget, to be expended by the Finance Committee to fund the snow and ice deficit or any other purpose authorized by M.G.L. Chapter 40, Section 6; or take any action thereon. Sponsored and Supported by the Select Board Finance Committee recommends adoption of this article ARTICLE 9. To see if the town will vote to transfer and appropriate from Free Cash the sum of $50,000 to the Special Education Stabilization Fund approved at May 13, 2025 Town Meeting, or take any action thereon. Sponsored and Supported by the Select Board Finance Committee recommends adoption of this article ARTICLE 10. To see if the Town will vote to create a special purpose stabilization fund to be known as the Capital Stabilization Fund, pursuant to the provisions of M.G.L. Chapter 40, Section 5B, the purpose of which shall be to provide a reserve for capital expenditures, including the repair, replacement, acquisition, or improvement of Town buildings, facilities, infrastructure, vehicles, or equipment, and for any other capital purpose, and to transfer and appropriate from Free Cash the sum of $458,142 for the initial deposit into said fund; or take any other action relative thereto. --2/3rd vote Sponsored and Supported by the Select Board Finance Committee recommends adoption of this article ARTICLE 11. To see if the Town will vote to transfer and appropriate from Free Cash the sum of $12,918 to be expended by the Town to fund bills from FY2025 for engineering services; or take any other action thereon. --4/5th vote Sponsored and Supported by the Select Board Finance Committee recommends adoption of this article 4 Annual Town Meeting, May 12, 2026 ARTICLE 12. To see if the Town will vote to transfer and appropriate from Free Cash the sum of $20,000 to be expended by the Select Board for feasibility analysis for siting cellular infrastructure on a parcel of land near the intersection of Main Street and Lawrence Road, including but not limited to survey and engineering services, and anything incidental or related thereto; or take any other action thereon. Sponsored and Supported by the Select Board Finance Committee recommends adoption of this article ARTICLE 13. To see if the Town will vote to amend the General Bylaws, Part I, Administrative Legislation, by inserting a new Chapter, Revolving Funds, to establish and authorize revolving funds for use by certain Town departments, boards, committees, agencies or officers under M.G.L. c. 44, §53E½, and further to create the Stiles Pond Beach Operations Revolving Fund, and to establish the Fiscal Year 2027 spending limit for said revolving fund, as shown below, or take any other action relative thereto. Part A: Revolving Fund Bylaw and Creation of Stiles Pond Beach Operations Revolving Fund DEPARTMENTAL REVOLVING FUNDS This bylaw establishes and authorizes revolving funds for use by Town departments, boards, committees, agencies or officers in connection with the operation of programs or activities that generate fees, charges or other receipts to support all or some of the expenses of those programs or activities. These revolving funds are established under and governed by M.G.L. c. 44, §53E½. Authorized Revolving Funds. Revolving Fund Stiles Pond Beach Operations Department, Board, Committee, Agency, or Officer Authorized to Spend Fund Town Administrator and Beach Director Revenue Source Expenses Payable from Fund Restrictions or Conditions on Expenses Payable from Fund Reporting and Other Requirements Seasonal Pass Program Stiles Pond Beach operations, including salaries and wages of lifeguards and beach personnel Revolving fund expenditures shall not be made to pay wages or salaries for full-time employees unless the revolving fund is also charged for the costs of fringe benefits associated with the wages or salaries so paid The Beach Director shall report on an annual basis on or before July 1st regarding the revenues generated by and expended from the Fund during each fiscal year. Spending Limits. Expenditures from each revolving fund set forth herein shall be subject to the limitation established annually by Town Meeting or any increase therein as may be authorized in accordance with G.L. c.44, §53E½. 5 Annual Town Meeting, May 12, 2026 Part B. Establish Fiscal Year 2027 Spending Limit Revolving Fund Stiles Pond Beach Operations Revolving Fund Fiscal Year 2027 Spending Limit $50,000 Sponsored and Supported by the Select Board Finance Committee recommends adoption of this article ARTICLE 14. To see if the Town will vote authorize the Select Board to adopt and amend from time to time a schedule of user fees for the use of Stiles Pond Beach, including but not limited to seasonal pass fees and other related charges; said fees to take effect as the Select Board may determine; or take any other action thereon. Sponsored and Supported by the Select Board Finance Committee recommends adoption of this article ARTICLE 15. To see if the Town will vote to authorize the Select Board to acquire by gift, or otherwise, parcels of land located on Hillside Road, being Assessor’s Map 20-13-06 and 20-13-07, Boxford, said property described in a deed recorded with the Essex South District Registry of Deeds in Book 6561, Page 292, for general municipal use, on such terms and conditions as the Select Board deems to be in the best interests of the Town; and, further, to authorize the Select Board to enter into all agreements and execute any and all instruments as may be necessary on behalf of the Town to carry out the purposes of this article, or take any other action thereon. Sponsored and supported by the Select Board Land Committee to make recommendation at Town Meeting ARTICLE 16. To see if the Town will vote to appropriate or reserve from the Community Preservation Fund annual revenues in the amounts recommended by the Community Preservation Committee for committee administrative expenses, debt service, community preservation projects and other expenses in Fiscal Year 2027, with each item to be considered a separate appropriation: Appropriations: From FY 2027 estimated annual revenues for Lincoln Hall Renovation Bond expense From FY 2027 estimated annual revenues for Haynes Land Purchase Bond expense From FY 2027 estimated annual revenues for Boxford Commons Bond expense From FY 2027 estimated annual revenues for 10 Elm Street Bond Expense From FY 2027 estimated annual revenues for Committee Administrative Expenses $36,444 $106,125 $118,500 $67,500 $66,062 Reserves: From FY 2027 estimated annual revenues for Community Housing Reserve From FY 2027 estimated annual revenues for Historic Reserve From FY 2027 estimated annual revenues for Open Space Reserve $132,134 $28,180 $27,999 6 Annual Town Meeting, May 12, 2026 From FY 2027 estimated annual revenues for Budgeted Reserve or take any other action thereon. $720,000 Sponsored and supported by the Community Preservation Committee Select Board recommends adoption of this article Finance Committee recommends adoption of this article ARTICLE 17. To see if the Town will vote to appropriate $3,190 from the Undesignated Community Preservation Fund balance to fund the purchase of soccer nets as part of the rehabilitation of Spofford Pond soccer field, said funds to be expended under the direction of the Boxford Parent Teacher Association in close coordination with the Town Administrator and Community Preservation Committee, or take any other action thereon. Sponsored and supported by the Community Preservation Committee Select Board recommends adoption of this article Finance Committee recommends adoption of this article ARTICLE 18. To see if the Town will vote to appropriate $25,000 from the Undesignated Community Preservation Fund balance and to authorize the reallocation of $19,912 in unspent funds from the June 2021 Annual Town Meeting Warrant Article 17, which appropriated $28,000 from the Community Preservation Committee Historic Fund balance to fund the preparation and drawings showing the historic rehabilitation of the Little Red School House, 26 Middleton Road, to be applied to the preparation of project specifications and bid documents and oversight of the construction project; with additional funds being provided from private donations, grants and contributions, that together will cover the remaining cost to complete the project, said funds to be expended under the direction of the Boxford Permanent Building Committee in coordination with the Friends of the Little Red School House and the Community Preservation Committee, or take any other action thereon. Sponsored and supported by the Community Preservation Committee Select Board recommends adoption of this article Finance Committee recommends adoption of this article ARTICLE 19. To see if the Town will vote to appropriate $1,000,000 from the Undesignated Community Preservation Fund balance to fund acquisition of parcels of land also known as the Barker Farm, being Map 4-1-2 and 1-1-1, conditioned upon Essex County Greenbelt holding title to these parcels in perpetuity, and the execution of a conservation restriction on the property to the satisfaction of the Community Preservation Committee and Select Board, said funds to be expended under the direction of Essex County Greenbelt Association, Inc. in close coordination with the Community Preservation Committee, or take any other action thereon. Sponsored and supported by the Community Preservation Committee Select Board to make recommendation at Town Meeting Finance Committee to make recommendation at Town Meeting 7 Annual Town Meeting, May 12, 2026 ARTICLE 20. To see if the Town will vote to appropriate $320,000 from the Undesignated Community Preservation Fund balance to fund the rehabilitation of baseball fields located at Carr Way as shown on Assessor’s Map 32-1-17, also known as Cargill Fields, and anything incidental or related thereto, with additional private funds provided for a total project cost of $350,000, said funds to be expended under the direction of the Boxford Little League in close coordination with the Town Administrator, and the Community Preservation Committee, or to take any other action thereon. Sponsored and supported by the Community Preservation Committee Select Board recommends adoption of this article Finance Committee recommends adoption of this article ARTICLE 21. To transact any other business that may legally come before said meeting. Supporting documents for this warrant may be found at: www.boxfordma.gov/TownMeeting2026 8 Annual Town Meeting, May 12, 2026 You are hereby ordered to notify and warn voters to meet in the Boxford Town Hall, 7A Spofford Road, Boxford, MA, on Tuesday, the 19th of May next, polls open from 7:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m., for the following purposes, viz: to choose by ballot the following Town Officers for the ensuing year: Select Board, ONE member for three years; Board of Assessors, ONE member for three years; Board of Health, TWO members for three years; Boxford School Committee, TWO members for three years; Masconomet Regional District School Committee, TWO members for three years, ONE member for 1 year; Planning Board, ONE member for four years, TWO members for five years; Board of Library Trustees, ONE member for three years; Town Moderator, ONE for three years; Constable, East Parish, ONE for three years, Constable, West Parish, ONE for three years; Board of Commissioners of Trust Funds, ONE member for three years; QUESTION #1: Shall the Town of Boxford be allowed to exempt from the provisions of proposition two and one-half, so-called, the amounts required to pay the Town’s allocable share of the bond issued by the Masconomet Regional School District for the purpose of paying feasibility study and schematic design costs related to a potential Accelerated Repair Project involving replacement of the roof and conversion of the HVAC system to heat pumps at Masconomet Middle School, located at 20 Endicott Rd in Boxford, MA, and replacement of the roof and conversion of the HVAC system to heat pumps at Masconomet High School, located at 20 Endicott Rd. in Boxford, MA, including the payment of all costs incidental or related thereto? text: TOWN OF DOVER ___ WARRANT for the ANNUAL TOWN MEETING Monday, May 4, 2026 and Monday, May 11, 2026 (should Town Meeting need to continue to a second evening) 7:00 PM Dover-Sherborn Regional High School Mudge Auditorium and TOWN ELECTIONS Monday, May 18, 2026 7:00 AM – 8:00 PM Dover Town House ARTICLES OF THE WARRANT ANNUAL TOWN MEETING 2026 To the Residents of Dover: This Warrant provides notification of the 2026 Annual Town Meeting and Town Election. It advises residents of the various issues being considered at the business meeting scheduled for May 4th and the Offices on the ballot for the Town Election on May 18th. Only Articles listed in this Warrant may come before residents for a vote. Articles for the Annual Town Meeting are grouped in four categories: Financial and Budget; Zoning, Planning, and Land Use; General Articles, and the Tax Rate. The most important votes that take place at the Annual Town Meeting are related to the budget. We urge citizens to read the budget, understand it, and help us foster excellence within the community. The Town website, https://www.doverma.gov/453/Town-Meeting, includes the most recent version of the FY2027 Budget and other financial Articles as well as other relevant information for each Article. A comprehensive budget recommendation for FY2027 will be delivered to all households in mid-April in the Warrant Committee Report and Recommendations for the Annual Town Meeting, also referred to as the ‘Blue Book’ (for its color). The Blue Book will provide much more detail and explanation of each Article. We recommend you bring a copy of the Blue Book to Town Meeting. About Town Meeting: Sometimes referred to as the oldest form of government in the country, Town Meeting is your opportunity to learn about, participate, and vote in Dover’s Town Government. Please consider spending a few hours of your time to attend this year’s Town Meeting and play a role in the direction of your Town. Thank you. Dover Board of Selectmen Robyn Hunter, Chair David M. Haviland, Clerk Cam Hudson, Member 2 ARTICLES OF THE WARRANT ANNUAL TOWN MEETING 2026 Norfolk, ss. Article 15. Article 16. Appropriate for One-Time Projects – Town-Wide Climate Action Plan (Sustainability Committee) To see if the Town will vote to raise and appropriate, appropriate from available funds, or any combination of these methods, a sum of money for the purpose of developing a Town-Wide Climate Action Plan, and to fund any incidental costs related thereto; or take any other action relative thereto. Article 20. Acceptance of Trail Easements (Open Space Committee) To see if the Town will vote to authorize the Board of Selectmen to accept a deed or deeds of easement interests, on such terms and conditions as the Board of Selectmen may determine and in final locations as the Board of Selectmen may determine for those certain easements in a subdivision known as the Ard Righ Estates being shown on a plan entitled “Ard Righ Estates, Dover, Massachusetts, Property of Dover Development Associates, 25 New Chardon St. Boston, Mass.” by Shurcliff, Morrill and Footit Landscape Architects, Boston, Mass., and R.E. text: COMMONWEALTH OF MASSACHUSETTS TOWN OF HULL Annual Town Meeting Monday, May 4, 2026 at 7:00 o’clock PM At the Hull High School situated at 180 Main Street, Hull, MA PLEASE BRING THIS DOCUMENT WITH YOU TO TOWN MEETING MODERATOR’S MESSAGE HULL ANNUAL TOWN MEETING MONDAY MAY 4, 2026, 7:00 p.m. HULL HIGH SCHOOL GYMNASIUM If you are a registered voter in Hull, I urge you to attend the Town Meeting and make your voice heard as we gather to decide the future direction of the town of Hull. The warrant you have received describes the Articles that will be discussed and voted on at Town Meeting. The actual vote will be on the motion presented at the Town Meeting and the motion is not necessarily the same as the article in the warrant. However, the motion must basically adhere in scope to the article presented in the warranty or it will be ruled out of order. Please take the time to review the warrant prior to Town Meeting, doing so will allow you to have a better understanding of the issue that will come before you at Town Meeting. One of the major items considered at each year’s Town Meeting is the annual budget and Town Meeting has the right to propose changes to the budget and any warrant article by offering amendments to any motion presented. A significant amount of work is done by Town departments and volunteer committees in preparing warrant articles. These articles and all budget requests are then forwarded to the Advisory Board who then spend two to three months reviewing the budgets department by department and all articles that come before Town Meeting. All department heads appear before the Advisory Board to explain and justify their budget requests once again. Things like zoning changes and Community Preservation Committee requests also come before the Advisory Board. Finally, the Advisory Board votes on each warrant article and makes a recommendation for your consideration at Town Meeting. However, the final decision rests with you, the citizens of Hull. Key items for consideration at this year’s Town Meeting include approval of the FY26 Operating Budget of $56,615,285.The town is proposing a number of capital projects to address needed facilities and infrastructure improvements. The Community Preservation Committee is proposing funding for renovations at the Carousel, Lifesaving Museum, Village Park Playground, Hull Community Garden, funding for the Hull Community Housing Trust and preservation of historic records, among others. A number of zoning bylaw changes are being proposed by the Planning Board for Town Meeting approval. Ten citizen petitions have also been filed this year covering a number of different areas. The eleven articles proposed as part of the Consent Agenda that follows this message. Articles on the Consent Agenda are done as a single vote without presentations or debate. At the request of seven or more Town Meeting members any article can be removed from the Consent Agenda and returned to the normal order of business. The rules at Town Meeting are straightforward and are geared to provide you with the opportunity to speak and vote on each of the motions presented at Town Meeting. The detailed procedure for running Town Meeting can be found in Town Meeting Times and a link to the Citizens Guide to Town Meeting can be found at the following link: https://www.town.hull.ma.us/sites/g/files/vyhlif3286/f/uploads/citizens_guide_to_town_meeting.pdf I will briefly explain the rules at the beginning of Town Meeting. I hope you will all take the opportunity to review the Warrant prior to Town Meeting and join me at the Annual Town Meeting at Hull High School on Monday, May 4, 2026, beginning at 7 p.m. George Boylen, /s/ George Boylen, Hull Town Moderator 2026 HULL ANNUAL TOWN MEETING PROPOSED CONSENT AGENDA ARTICLE 1: Acceptance of reports. TOWN OF HULL Advisory Board 253 Atlantic Avenue Hull, Massachusetts 02045 781-925-2000 To the Citizens of Hull, Starting with the 2024 Town Meeting we have used a “Consent Agenda” in Town Meeting. The Consent Agenda allows the Moderator, in consultation with the Chair of the Select Board and the Chair of the Advisory Board, to combine Articles that are deemed “not likely to be controversial and not likely to generate debate” into one motion that can be passed with a simple majority. Seven or more voters in attendance may hold or remove an item from the Consent Agenda(s), to be acted on in the normal manner. The remaining Articles in the Consent Agenda will then be voted on as one motion without presentation or debate. You will see housekeeping Articles, and some of the Enterprise Fund Authorizations. These are standard Articles that we must pass each year. This Warrant contains a Projected Revenue and Expenditure Summary for the Fiscal Year ending June 30, 2027. This Summary reflects a balanced budget achieved by diligent work of all Town Departments. This enables the Town to maintain services. As has been mentioned in previous years, we look for all Town Departments to work within a budget and manage accordingly. This will be the seventh (7th) year that the Community Preservation Committee presents projects for appropriation of funds derived via the Community Preservation Act adopted by the Town. The collaboration of all Town Departments, boards, committees, and employees serves the Town of Hull well. We are immensely proud of their dedication. This process usually concludes with agreement between the Advisory Board and the Town Manager in terms of presenting the budget to Town Meeting. The Advisory Board considers all Articles for the purpose of making recommendations with explanatory statements. While considering each Article many questions are considered such as: Is it necessary? Can the Town afford it? Is it in the Town's best interest? Is it fair to all? Does it affect the balance of power? Is it within legal and allowable guidelines? The Special Town Meeting will cover business matters that must be acted upon before the end of this fiscal year, which is June 30, 2026. During the annual Town Meeting, the citizens of Norwell will vote on a budget for Fiscal Year 2027, as well as many other matters of interest to the Town. We encourage Town residents to review the Warrant. Voters attending Town Meeting responsibly discuss, debate, and determine Norwell’s budget for the upcoming year. The Advisory Board’s role is to advise residents of its recommendations on each Article contained in this Warrant. These recommendations have been determined following several months of evaluation and careful consideration of all the materials provided by Town Departments, Boards, and Committees. Every proposed article was reviewed by the Advisory Board with a presentation from its proponents in a public meeting. The intent of the budget is to provide appropriate funds to support ongoing operations, address capital and infrastructure needs, and maintain the Town’s fiscal health. All departments, boards, and committees continue to work with a common purpose to identify efficiencies and methods to better address budgetary challenges while delivering services to the residents of the Town of Norwell. We would like to thank the residents, employees, and volunteers across all Departments, Boards, and Committees for their invaluable input. In particular, we extend our gratitude to Ellen McKenna for her exceptional support to the Advisory Board. We also wish to formally thank Christine McCarthy, Finance Director, for her professional guidance and dedicated support throughout this entire process. We extend special thanks to Darleen Sullivan, Town Administrator, who is retiring after many years of outstanding service to the Town of Norwell. Her leadership, expertise, and unwavering commitment have been instrumental in guiding the Town through countless challenges and successes, and we are deeply grateful for her many contributions. It is important that your voice is heard. We look forward to seeing you at Town Meeting on May 4, 2026. Sincerely, The Norwell Advisory Board John LaCara, Chair Bob Perniola, Vice Chair Stephen Bright Patricia Grueter Matthew Hanson Lucas Hamory Bob Howard Ann Mulligan Matthew Weinmann 4 TOWN BUDGET Glossary of Terms Appropriation: An authorization to make expenditures and to incur obligations for specific purposes. An appropriation is granted by Town Meeting and is usually limited in time and amount as to when it may be expended. Any part of the general appropriation not spent or encumbered by June 30 automatically reverts to surplus. A specific appropriation is carried forward from year to year until spent for the designated purpose or transferred by Town Meeting vote to another account. Assessed Valuation: A valuation set upon real or personal property by the Board of Assessors as a basis for levying taxes. Budget: A plan of financial operation consisting of an estimate of proposed expenditures for a given period and the means of financing them. The budget is voted in the spring at Town Meeting for the fiscal year that begins the following July 1st. Capital Budget: A plan of proposed capital outlays and the means of financing them for the current year. Cherry Sheet: An annual statement received from the Massachusetts Department of Revenue detailing estimated receipts for the next fiscal year and the estimated state and county government charges payable. These amounts are used by the assessors in setting the tax rate. The actual receipts and charges may vary from the estimates. Community Preservation Act (CPA): The Town adopted the Community Preservation Act (CPA) in 2002. This Act allows the town to collect a 3% surcharge on property tax bills (the funds can be matched up to 100% by the state when funds are available), which creates the Community Preservation Fund, to use for Community Preservation purposes. Each year, the town must appropriate, or reserve (but not necessarily spend), 10% of the funds for each of the three Community Preservation purposes: Open Space, Historic Resources, and Community Housing. The remaining 70% of the funds can be appropriated, reserved or used for any of the three purposes and for Recreation and administration. Debt Service: Payment of interest and repayment of principal to holders of the Town’s debt instruments. Fiscal Year: A 12-month period, commencing July 1 and ending June 30, to which the annual budget applies. Fiscal years are often denoted FYXX with the last two numbers representing the calendar year in which it ends, for example FY25 is the fiscal year ended June 30, 2025. Free Cash: Free cash is the portion of unreserved fund balance available for appropriation. 5 It is not cash but rather is approximately the total of cash and receivables, less current liabilities and earmarked reserves, reduced also by reserves for uncollected taxes. This is also referred to as “available cash”. The amount is certified annually by the Massachusetts Department of Revenue. General Fund: The major town owned fund which is created with town receipts and which is charged with expenditures payable from revenues. Grant: A contribution of assets by one governmental unit or other organization to another. Typically, these contributions are made to local governments from the state and federal governments. Grants are usually made for specific purposes. Line-Item Budget: A format of budgeting that organizes costs by type of expenditure such as expenses, equipment, and salaries. Overlay: The amount set aside to allow for uncollected property taxes. An amount for overlay is added to the appropriations and other charges. The “Overlay Surplus” is the portion of each year’s overlay account no longer required to cover property tax abatements. Overlay Surplus: The unused amount of the overlay for prior years, which may be transferred, by vote of the Town, to the reserve account or used for any lawful purpose. Property Tax Levy: The amount produced by multiplying the assessed valuation of property by the tax rate. The tax rate is expressed “per thousand dollars” of assessed valuation. Reserve Fund: Money set aside by Town Meeting to be allocated by the Advisory Board for extraordinary or unforeseen expenditures. Stabilization Fund: A special reserve funded by Town Meeting for future expenditures. The Town has also established Athletic Fields Stabilization, Capital Stabilization and Special Education Stabilization funds. Terms associated with Proposition 2½: Debt or Capital Exclusion: The Town can assess taxes in excess of the levy limit by voting a debt exclusion or capital outlay exclusion. This amount does not become a permanent part of the levy limit base, but allows the Town to assess taxes for a specific period of time in excess of the limit for payment of debt service costs or for payment of capital expenditures. Excess Levy Capacity: The difference between the Town's tax levy limit and its actual tax levy for the current year. It is the additional tax levy that could be raised without asking for an override. New Growth: The amount of property tax revenue that the Town can add to its allowable tax levy as a result of new construction, alterations, subdivisions or change of use, which 6 increases the value of a parcel of land by more than certain amounts. Override: An amount voted by the Town, which is permanently added to the levy limit. A majority vote of the Selectmen allows an override question to be put on the ballot. Town Meeting remains the cornerstone of our local democracy, providing residents with the opportunity to directly participate in the decisions that shape our community. We encourage all eligible voters to attend, ask questions, and take part in the important work before us. This year’s Warrant reflects a careful balance between maintaining essential services, investing in critical infrastructure, and exercising fiscal discipline. The Town continues to face significant financial pressures, including rising costs associated with health insurance, special education, and other fixed obligations. As a result, difficult decisions were required to prioritize needs over wants, defer certain initiatives, and focus on the long-term financial stability of the Town. Among the articles presented are several important capital and infrastructure investments, including applying for and accepting state roadway funds and grants for improvements, water system upgrades, and public safety equipment, many of which leverage state or federal funding opportunities. The Warrant also includes zoning updates, policy refinements, and other measures intended to support thoughtful growth and enhance the quality of life in Plainville. We thank the Finance Committee, Town staff, and our boards and committees for their hard work in developing the articles and recommendations contained in this Warrant. We look forward to a productive and respectful Town Meeting and appreciate your continued engagement and commitment to the Town of Plainville. This has been a particularly challenging budget cycle. The Town continues to experience significant cost increases in areas largely outside of local control, including health insurance, special education, retirement obligations, and contractual commitments. At the same time, revenue growth remains constrained under Proposition 2½, slow new growth and diminishing state aid, requiring the Committee to make difficult decisions to ensure that the budget remains balanced. In response to these pressures, the Committee worked closely with Town staff and departments to prioritize essential services and core municipal functions. An appropriation is granted by Town Meeting and is usually limited in time and amount as to when it may be expended. Any part of the general appropriation not spent or encumbered by June 30th automatically reverts to surplus, which may become Free Cash. A specific appropriation is carried forward from year to year until spent for the designated purpose or transferred by Town Meeting vote to another account. Assessed Valuation: A valuation set upon real or personal property by the Board of Assessors as a basis for levying taxes. Budget: A plan of financial operation consisting of an estimate of proposed expenditures for a given period and the means of financing them. The budget is voted at the Annual Town Meeting for the fiscal year that begins the following July 1st. Capital Budget: A plan of proposed capital outlays and the means of financing them for the current year. Cherry Sheet: An annual statement received from the Massachusetts Department of Revenue detailing estimated payments to the Town for the next fiscal year and the estimated state and county government charges payable by the Town. The Assessors in setting the tax rate use these amounts. The actual receipts and charges may vary from the estimates. Community Preservation Act (CPA): The Town adopted the Community Preservation Act (CPA) in 2019. This Act allows the Town to collect up to a 3% surcharge (Plainville has voted 1%) on property tax bills (the funds can be matched up to 100% by the state when funds are available), which creates the Community Preservation Fund, to use for Community Preservation purposes. Each year, the town must appropriate, or reserve (but not necessarily spend), 10% of the funds for each of the three Community Preservation purposes: Open Space, Historic Resources, and Community Housing. The remaining 70% of the funds can be appropriated or reserved for any of the three purposes and for Recreation and/or for administration. Consent Agenda: A consent agenda’s purpose is to act expeditiously upon certain types of articles that historically have generated no controversy and can reasonably be voted upon without debate. With a consent agenda, several articles can be addressed with a single vote, thereby ensuring that a greater proportion of the town meeting's time is dedicated to articles that are the subject of genuine debate. See the Appendix in the back of this Town Meeting Warrant. Debt or Capital Exclusion: The Town can assess taxes in excess of the levy limit by voting a debt exclusion or capital outlay exclusion. This amount does not become a permanent part of the levy limit base but does allow the Town to assess taxes for a specific period in excess of the limit for payment of debt service costs or payment of capital expenditures. Debt Service: Payment of interest and repayment of principal to holders of the Town’s debt. Enterprise Fund: An Enterprise Fund is a type of municipal accounting mechanism used to manage the finances of a specific service or utility—such as water, sewer, or solid waste (trash and recycling) —in a manner similar to a private business. Under an enterprise fund, all revenues and expenses associated with providing the service are tracked separately from the general fund. The service is intended to be self-supporting, meaning that user fees and charges (rather than taxes) are the primary funding source. 6|Page This approach promotes transparency and ensures that the true cost of providing the service is visible to both administrators and ratepayers. It allows for better long-term financial planning, including capital investment, maintenance, and debt service for the utility. Enterprise funds are authorized under MGL Chapter 44, Section 53F½ and must be formally adopted by Town Meeting. Once established, the fund operates with its own budget, and any surplus (retained earnings) may be used for future utility-related needs, subject to appropriation. Excess Levy Capacity: The difference between the Town’s tax levy limit and its actual tax levy for the current year. It is the additional tax levy that could be raised without asking for an override. Fiscal Year: A 12-month period, commencing July 1 and ending June 30th, to which the annual budget applies. Fiscal years are often denoted FYXX with the last two numbers representing the calendar year in which it ends, for example, FY27 is the fiscal year ending June 30, 2027. Free Cash: Free cash is the portion of the unreserved fund balance available for appropriation. It is not cash but rather is approximately the total of cash and receivables less current liabilities and earmarked reserves also reduced by reserves for uncollected taxes. This is also referred to as “available cash”. The amount is certified annually by the Massachusetts Department of Revenue. General Fund: The major town-owned fund is created with town receipts and is charged with expenditures payable from revenues. Grant: A contribution of assets by one governmental unit or other organization to another. Typically, these contributions are made to local governments from the state and federal governments. Grants are usually made for specific purposes. Line-Item Budget: A format of budgeting that organizes costs by type of expenditure such as expenses, equipment, and salaries. New Growth: The amount of property tax revenue that the Town can add to its allowable tax levy as a result of new construction, alterations, subdivisions or change of use which increases the value of a parcel of land by more than certain amounts. OPEB: Other Post-Employment Benefits. Benefits that an employee of the Town will receive in retirement. OPEB does not include pension benefits paid to the retired employee. Other benefits include insurance premiums, healthcare premiums, and deferred-compensation contractual arrangements. Overlay: The amount set aside to allow for uncollected property taxes. An amount for the overlay is added to the appropriations and other charges. Overlay Surplus – see below. Overlay Surplus: The unused amount of the overlay from prior years, which may be transferred, by a vote of the Town, to the reserve account or used for extraordinary items. Override: An amount, voted by the Town, which is permanently added to the levy limit. A majority vote of the Select Board allows an override question to be put on the ballot. Override questions must be presented in dollar terms and must specify the purpose of the override. Overrides require a majority vote of approval by the Town. Property Tax Levy: The amount produced by multiplying the assessed valuation of property by the tax rate. The tax rate is expressed “per thousand dollars” of assessed valuation. 7|Page Reserve Fund: Money set aside by Town Meeting to be allocated by the Finance Committee for extraordinary or unforeseen expenditures. Stabilization Fund: A special reserve funded by Town Meeting for future expenditures. Tax Classification Tax Allocation: Before setting the tax rate each year, a classification hearing is held by the Select Board to determine the shares of the tax levy to be paid by each class of property in the community, and whether to allow an open space discount, residential exemption, or small commercial exemption. The Assessors provide information about the impact of these options at the hearing. The decisions of the Select Board are reported to the Bureau of Accounts and are referred to as the “Classification Tax Allocation.” Tax Levy Limit: The maximum amount of the tax levy for a period under the restrictions of Proposition 2½. Because it is difficult for all taxpayers to be completely informed about every aspect of a Town’s finances, Fincoms were established so a representative group of taxpayers could conduct a thorough review of municipal finance questions on behalf of all citizens.” With this in mind, the Fincom’s primary responsibility is advisory, to examine the budget and all other warrant articles and make recommendations to the voters on each article. It also administers the Reserve Fund ($80,000) to provide for urgent and unforeseen expenditures that might arise between Town meetings. Lastly, although it is not required in our Charter, the Finance Committee Annual Report provides the Voters with an overview of the Town’s financial condition. In Stow, the Moderator appoints five voting members and up to five associate members to the Finance Committee. Any voter registered in Stow is eligible to join. As of the publication date, there are five voting members and one associate members on the committee. Town Revenues Town revenues totaled $37,478,124 in FY25, a 2.53% increase from FY24, with property taxes continuing to dominate revenue generation for the town. The recent downward trend in tax rate has been offset by the continued increase in property values. The tax revenue collected for FY25 was $34,455,790. Local receipts were collected totaling $2,473,436, and State Aid was $548,898. Most notably, revenues from state aid were down sharply (-31%) from FY24. Town Expenditures The town continues to demonstrate a commitment to maintaining the budgetary targets supported at the annual Town Meeting. Expenditures for FY25 totaled $34,778,145, an increase of $2,430,091 (7.51%) compared to FY24. As is usual, these expenditures were dominated by assessments from our two local school districts, followed by municipal operating costs, and debt servicing. Town Savings Town savings (Free Cash plus the Stabilization Fund) are “rainy day” accounts that are built up during good times and drawn down in bad times. Free Cash comes from receiving more-thanbudget revenue (taxes, state aid, budget money left over from the prior year) and/or spending less than our voted budget. It is annually certified each year by the Department of Revenue (DOR). 5 Fiscal Year 2025 2024 2023 2022 2021 2020 Free Cash $2,075,156 $3,276,056 $1,876,404 $2,049,610 $2,385,510 $2,897,441 % of budget Stabilization fund 5.97% 10% 5.38% 6.18% 7.45% 8.87% % of budget $1,691,393 $1,413,559 $950,339 $739,085 $523,077 $520,971 4.86 4.19% 2.73% 2.23% 1.63% 1.59% Total 3,766,549.00 4,689,615.00 2,826,743.00 2,788,695.00 2,908,587.00 3,418,412.00 Once certified, free cash is available for appropriation throughout the fiscal year, to be spent for any lawful purpose. Every dollar of free cash appropriated as revenue in the FY25 budget is a dollar that does not need to be raised and appropriated through taxation. These savings are a necessity, not a luxury, and accumulate to build a targeted balance or used to fund the next year’s budget. In discussions with Standard and Poor’s leading up to our AAA rating approval, which was reaffirmed in October of 2025, the Town was encouraged to attempt to maintain a stored asset balance of between 5% and 10% of the overall budget (10.8%). The Town has achieved our initial OPEB funding target of 20% of total liability. 6 Fiscal Year FY25 FY24 FY23 FY22 FY21 FY20 FY19 FY18 Current OPEB Liability OPEB Savings % Of Liability $2,195,196.00 22.91% $1,771,195.00 19.46% $1,389,340.00 14.96% $1,081,675.00 11.65% $822,807.00 8.86% $577,144.00 6.21% $329,296.00 3.55% $218,453.00 2.35% $9,580,357.00 Fiscal Year 2027 Proposed Budget Analysis Looking forward to the 2027 requested budget and comparing to the 2026 voter-approved budget, key highlights are as follows: ● Total revenue is estimated at $44,929,970 including unused levy capacity. The primary contributor to the revenue estimates is property tax. Of the $44.9M, approximately $40.5M is attributable to property tax, inclusive of the prop 2 ½ increase allowance. New growth revenue at is projected at $200,000, down 13.8% from FY26. A projected total FY27 levy limit revenue of $35,350,400 represents a 3.08% increase over FY26. ● Based on the initial indications from the State regarding State Aide Revenue, we are only estimating a small increase of 3.91% (~$20k). Continuing the trend of the past few years State contributions to cities and towns has remained relatively flat compared to revenue at the State level. ● Revenue from local receipts (motor vehicle excise tax, permit fees, license fees, etc) is projected to increase 5.95% in FY27. This number is conservative, as we expect Masters Academy to come online and several developments to break ground in FY27. ● The Town Administrator is proposing to use $1,402,375 of Free Cash in FY27, which will be applied to the following: o Transfer $300 into the Stabilization Fund; o Transfer $100k into the Capital Stabilization Fund; o Contribute $235k to the OBEP Trust Fund; o Use $867,375 to fund the Capital Plan ● We also expect to need a transfer on Town Meeting floor to cover the remainder of the snow & ice deficit. At this time, that figure is not known. Once we see what we’ll have for available General Fund funds, we’ll have a final deficit amount. ● FY2027 expenditures are dominated, as is typical, by the Nashoba school assessment at 58.29% of expenditures, followed by the municipal budget (including insurance) at 27.21%, municipal debt service at 7.89%, and the Minuteman assessment at 6.62%. As with all three towns in the Nashoba regional district, Stow’s educational expenses are a substantial portion of the total expenditures in any given year. As an aggregate, inclusive of debt servicing, Education accounts for 67% of the operating budget. 7 ● Total expenditure is expected to increase by 1.92% above FY26 spending. While the Nashoba assessment remains the largest line item, we are happy to report that the projected assessment increase of 2.93% by Nashoba was partially offset by a 7.02% reduction by Minuteman. The budget requests include a 5.94% increase in the municipal budget, a 50% reduction in capital expenses, and a 5% increase in special article expenditures. ● The net increase for the FY27 budget is 4.22% over the FY26. In the Fall of 2025, the Town Administrator put before Special Town Meeting an adjustment to the Wage & Classification Schedule for non-union employees. This proposal had the Finance Committee’s support and overwhelmingly passed Town Meeting. The wage increases in this budget are primarily a result of those changes with relatively little increase in department expenses. Stow continues to operate very conservatively, with limited nonessential expenses in our municipal budget. For FY27, the Select Board renegotiated the Town Administrator’s contract; as a result of the market rate for the TA position, an increase has been budgeted for. This increase will bring salary in line with the median. However, she will still be far below the median for total compensation in the region. This increase represents 1.76% of the municipal increase. While this increase may appear large, the Finance Committee acknowledges the impact and dedication of our current TA. As such, the Finance Committee supports this pay adjustment to bring the Town Administrator closer to the median market value for her position. Fiscal Year 2027 Special Articles – Raise & Appropriate Special articles have increased from $496,150 to $520,850 – an increase of less than 5%. Some highlights to the special articles are: ● A $30,000 (50%) reduction in the cost of operating the municipal water supply serving town-owned properties. ● $15,000 to digitally archive permanent records, including documents, plans, and permit information. Fiscal Year 2027 Capital Articles In the past, year-over-year capital expenditure was primarily by allocation of CPC funds. Omitting the CPC fund usage, significant contributors to the capital allocation are the town’s need to replace aging vehicles and critical infrastructure. We have benefited from the ability to maintain vehicles for extended periods, with highway equipment having service lifetimes upwards of 30 years. However, the combination of deferred replacements and drastically increased delivery timelines is forcing us to be more proactive with regards to key pieces of highway equipment and other municipal vehicles (police cruiser, ambulance, fire engines). As some vehicles are experiencing a 12 year backorder, we must appropriate funds and get in the replacement queue in order to ensure we are able to continue providing essential services. 8 In FY27, the Town administrator is Administrator is proposing we procure a number of vehicles through borrowing. This will allow us to sign a purchase order, but not hold up cash, while we wait one to two years for delivery. It will also allow us to repair aging infrastructure within the general fund budget, while budgeting for a principal and interest payment over a number of years and not all at once. Notably, the proposal includes this borrowing within the tax levy and not as debt exclusion. The remainder of the capital plan, as proposed, will be supported through appropriation from free cash and CPC funds. This diversified approach to funding our capital needs will be central to maintaining the financial health and critical infrastructure of Stow in FY27 and beyond. Conclusion Coupled with the growth in housing prices, the Town-wide valuation has grown faster than our costs (i.e. budget expenditures growth), allowing the Town to fund approved projects and capital items for the last several years. Moreover, the Town continues to maintain enough stored assets to benefit from low interest rates on borrowing due to our AAA rating. In addition, Stow has a certified excess levy capacity of approximately $1.62 million. As previously mentioned, this allows the town to borrow money at a more favorable rate. It is our opinion that this is a fair and accurate picture of the Town’s financial state. Whether you are pleased or displeased, the Finance Committee reminds everyone that Town Meeting directly controls the rate of growth of Town expenses. We encourage your participation. Respectfully submitted, Brian Patuto (Chair), Ross Perry (Member), Tom Farnsworth (Member), Angela Zhang (Member), Jeff Kimmelman (Member), John Mulroy (Associate Member) 9 TOWN ADMINISTRATOR’S FY27 BUDGET RECOMMENDATION LETTER Town of Stow Office of the Town Administrator Denise M. Dembkoski, Town Administrator Re: FY27 Budget Recommendations Date: March 31, 2026 The Fiscal Year 2027 (FY27) Operating Budget process provided an opportunity for management to, once again, undertake an honest assessment of town functions to determine what is working and what changes are necessary. Some of the recommended changes contained within this memorandum will have cost implications for the FY27 budget, but unfortunately, they are unavoidable. We are facing large increases in facility work and health insurance. At the Special Town Meeting in October 2025, I presented changes to the Wage and Classification Schedule to eliminate the first four steps of the scale and add four steps to the higher end of the scale. This would cause those employees in the first four steps to be reclassified to what is the new Step 1 (originally step 5) and employees who had been maxed out at then Step 12, would be reclassified to Step 8 and have additional step increases available to them. These changes impacted 11 employees on the low end of the ranges. In addition, 7 employees, who were maxed out, and had not received a step increase in a few years, will now receive one. All other employees are handled as usual, either receiving their Step and/or COLA increase. This year, in addition to the 2% Cost of Living Adjustment (COLA), all employees in Grades 6 – 8, will be granted a step increase. During the negotiations, we determined that the members of the fire union were paid well below the median for area firefighters, so there is a base wage adjustment factored into the budget, to bring them up to competitive salaries. There are two non-union contracts also up for June 30, 2026. One is for the Police Lieutenant and the other is for my contract. Both contracts have been successfully renegotiated and ratified by the Select Board, with all financial implications included in the budget recommendation. 10 For the FY27 budget, here are some key changes: The majority of the increases are the implementation of the new Salary Classification Plan, with many being the pay adjustments and 11 employees, who now receive a step increase. Dear Truro Voters: Message from the Moderator On May 16th, we will gather as a community at the 2026 Annual Town Meeting. This year marks the 250th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence. Town Meeting is perhaps the purest expression of the practice of self-governance envisioned by the authors of the Declaration. We have an opportunity at each Town Meeting to uphold democratic principles. To not just show but prove that the voices of everyone matter. That it is possible to account for differences and make tough decisions as a collective while being honest, kind, civil and respectful. Disagreement and difference are not a failure of democracy – they are evidence that it is working as long as decisions are based in listening, learning and compromise - moving us towards consensus rather than division. We will be casting our votes electronically at this year’s Annual Town Meeting as an opportunity to fully experience and explore this voting method as recommended by voters last year. At the conclusion of the meeting a vote will be taken to recommend whether to use electronic voting at future Town Meetings. Whether we wave a colored voting card or press a button on an electronic device, we are still legislating, and the power of each vote remains unchanged. While we may not be raising our hands this year please don’t let that stop you from raising your voice - once recognized - to speak to the issues at hand as presented in the Warrant. Please take time to read each of the articles fully as well as the motion book when it becomes available. You’ll also find information about our traditions, process, and procedures in this Warrant. If you have questions about Town Meeting process, please feel free to reach out to me. Lastly, let’s offer one another what we would wish for ourselves – to be heard and considered, with respect and openness, and to remember that those sitting around us are neighbors who also care deeply about Truro. I look forward to seeing you at Annual Town Meeting on May 16th. Paul Wisotzky Town Moderator moderator@truro-ma.gov Here are a few helpful guidelines for this year’s Annual Town Meeting: • In order to accommodate all voters, the meeting will be held under a large, heated tent at Truro Central School.
