You can find more information and announcements about this specific meeting and Town Meeting in general on the Town of Truro website on the Town Meeting Information page. 5|Page Annual Town Meeting – Saturday, May 16, 2026 Dear Truro Voter: INTRODUCTION Message from the Select Board As we continue to plan for increased participation in town meetings, the 2026 Annual Town Meeting will convene under a tent on the Truro Central School ballfield once again this year. The physical layout of the meeting will look very similar to the past couple of years but this year will have one new element—electronic voting. With the favorable advisory vote at last year’s town meeting, the Town Moderator, Select Board Chair and Town staff have worked diligently to bring this new technology to this year’s town meeting to increase voter privacy, meeting efficiency and vote count accuracy. While this is a departure from the traditions that our legislative body, town meeting, is used to, we hope that it will be a great success. As prescribed by the Charter, the warrant was prepared under the direction of the Select Board. A series of operating budget articles are presented at the start of the Warrant and include the omnibus budget appropriation, free cash transfers for current year expenses related to snow removal, and free cash transfers for the upcoming fiscal year. These free cash transfers are typically used for non-recurring or short-term expenses, or to put money away for larger purchases, “rainy day” savings (general stabilization fun), or long-term liabilities (OPEB). The largest free cash transfer request is for $1,000,000 to put toward a new public works facility. If approved, this reduces the amount needed to borrow, thus lessening the burden on taxpayers. Other free cash transfer sections include funding a second year of the Senior Perks Pilot Program, funding the Climate Action Coordinator position (in advance of solar revenues being realized), subsidizing the fuel costs in the operating budget due to market volatility, funding evaluation costs for land swaps with the Cape Cod National Seashore, and funding the costs of electronic voting at our next town meeting. One of the most highly anticipated articles this year is the borrowing authorization for the new public works facility. As promised last year, the Select Board determined that the best course forward was to bid the construction project, select the bid, and then to prepare a Town Meeting article that is based on the actual bid amount, which it has done. This eliminates the uncertainty of how much the project will cost and allows construction to move forward almost immediately after voters approve the project at Town Meeting and at the ballot. This project, in the making for ten years, is one of the Select Board’s most important priorities. The health and safety of our employees, the protection of the town’s assets, the need to address the current facilities that are falling deeper and deeper into disrepair, and the continuously rising construction costs make this vote critical. Thanks to the efforts of the Ad Hoc Building Committee, a thoughtfully and carefully considered building is proposed that balances the needs of the department with the needs of the taxpayers. A consent agenda with customary, procedural articles is again presented this year for meeting expediency. It bundles six articles that occur each year and are “housekeeping” in nature. Ten Community Preservation Act articles are included in the warrant as stand-alone articles. Two articles seek to update the Non-Union Personnel Bylaw, bringing parity between non-union and clerical union employees’ vacation and longevity bonus schedules. Two articles related to easements are presented that would allow the town to grant an easement for utilities to the Cloverleaf housing project and would allow the town to acquire an easement for public water supply well for Town Hall Hill. A General Bylaw amendment that memorializes the terms of the Truro Affordable Housing Trust, in accordance with the 2022 Annual Town Meeting vote to accept the General Law allowing the town to establish the trust is also included. A series of zoning bylaw amendments were prepared by three separate groups—the Planning Board, the Ad Hoc Zoning Task Force, and the Planning Department. The proposed articles seek to clarify portions of the Zoning Bylaws, bring the Zoning Bylaws into compliance with State requirements (namely the Seasonal Communities Act), and to propose ways to increase housing opportunities, housing production and economic development. A home rule petition is proposed for fertilizer reduction that would help reduce the town’s controllable nitrogen load and would mirror similar efforts in surrounding towns. Articles to remove the checkbox on tax bills that 6|Page Annual Town Meeting – Saturday, May 16, 2026 INTRODUCTION requests donations for the Elderly and Disabled Taxation Fund and to appropriate funds from the Cemetery Sale of Lots of Fund for extraordinary maintenance needs are also included in the warrant. Six articles were submitted by citizen petition: two zoning articles related to the Walsh Overlay District approved at the 2025 Annual Town Meeting, one zoning article seeking to re-instate the Growth Management Bylaw, one declaration of the Right to Farm and Fish, one article seeking to require voter approval for any changes to dog regulations, and one article reauthorizing a previously-approved solar array borrowing authorization for the purpose of adding rooftop solar at the proposed public works facility. Finally, after using the new electronic voting devices, voters will be asked to advise the Select Board on the continued use of the devices, thus setting the course for the next town meeting. We thank you in advance for your patience and adherence to directions to maintain order throughout the meeting as we implement this technology and manage the anticipated large voter turnout. We look forward to seeing you all for the 2026 Annual Town Meeting. Truro Select Board Susan Areson, Chair Susan Girard-Irwin, Vice-Chair Nancy Medoff, Clerk Stephanie Rein John Dundas 7|Page Annual Town Meeting – Saturday, May 16, 2026 To All Truro Voters: INTRODUCTION Message from the Finance Committee As mandated by Massachusetts’ law, the Finance Committee (“Committee”) functions as the town’s official fiscal watchdog. As such, the Committee’s primary responsibility is to study, analyze, and offer recommendations to the Town Meeting with regard to Truro’s Annual Budget, Capital Improvement Plan, and any financial warrant articles, as well as to understand and to monitor the process for setting the town tax rate. The Committee must also review and approve all proposed reserve fund transfers for unanticipated expenses. In performing these responsibilities during 2025 and 2026, the Committee held a number of public meetings, including several joint meetings with the Select Board, and one public Budget Hearing. The Committee also participated in the Budget Task Force (“The Task Force”), which was established several years ago to gain a better understanding of departmental spending and budget requests. The Task Force consists of two members of the Finance Committee, two members of the Select Board, the Town Manager, Finance Director, the Town Accountant and the Superintendent of Schools. The Task Force met a number of times throughout the winter of 2026. The meetings are open to the public and televised to allow interested taxpayers to observe the formation of the budget in process. The Omnibus Annual Budget for Fiscal Year 2027 totals $28,450,124.83 which is an increase of $749,334.83 or 2.7% from the adopted FY2026 budget. Transfers of Free Cash in support of annual omnibus budget items are not included in either figure. We continue to seek more control over the escalating costs by taking a holistic look at the budget to gain a better understanding of synergies that exist within town departments and among the entire Outer Cape community. The Committee believes that the proposed budget is needed to deliver the services recommended by the Select Board to the taxpayers. The budget was constructed based on conservative guidelines issued by the Select Board and supported by the Committee. Increases in the budget are largely due to increases in the cost of public safety, existing services and adequate compensation including contractual salary obligations, and community sustainability. As in prior years, the majority of the budget is made up of salaries, employee benefits, energy costs, and education. Since it is difficult to influence spending in the short term in these areas, prudent decisions must be made that will have long-term impact. The Committee encourages continued discussion among community members, Select Board, Town Manager, Finance Committee and town staff on ways in which to collaborate and share resources among neighboring communities. The Committee believes these efforts may result in more effective delivery of services. Absent substantive change in the way we currently deliver services as a region, costs will continue to escalate. It is incumbent upon leadership to take steps to stabilize the budget. This can be accomplished in a variety of ways. Housing initiatives that accommodate year-round and seasonal workers reduces wage pressure and the need for signing bonuses; the construction of an adequate DPW facility eliminates emergency building repairs and extends the useful life of vehicles and equipment, providing a safe work environment; measures to expand the year-round population creates economic stimulus and stabilizes the overall economy. The FY ’27 budget contains a number of recommendations intended to accomplish these goals. The Committee believes it is important to acknowledge the positive impact these initiatives represent.
